[The Start of Previous Conversation]
user: Why big clients want the contractor to be incorporated before giving them work
assistant: Big clients may require a contractor to be incorporated as a way of distancing themselves from the contractor to ensure they are not responsible for any monies if the contractor doesn't pay their taxes.  Additionally, incorporation helps to distance company assets from the contractor's personal assets.  They feel more protected when their contracts are incorporated.  It adds legal credibility as a contractor.  However, if the clients are not requiring incorporation, the contractor can simply act as a sole proprietorship.
user: Does it mean contractors have to purchase their own insurance and medicals, and of course taxes?
assistant: Yes, if you file a Schedule C as a self-employed person, you can buy medical insurance for yourself as an employment benefit and pay for it out of the income of the Schedule C business, thus saving on taxes.
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
Tax rate for LLC
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
LLC is not a federal tax designation. It's a state-level organization.  The tax rate for an LLC depends on the State where the business is registered, as well as the individual's overall taxable income. Some States, like Wyoming, an LLC is a pass-through entity without income tax, while others, like California, impose a franchise tax of $800 per year and income tax on gross revenue. 
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
LLC 的税率取决于所在州，参考内容没有提供统一税率。以加州为例，LLC 每年仅因存在就需缴纳 800 美元特许经营税，此外还可能按总收入缴纳所得税。怀俄明州则据称没有税，只有注册费，通常约为每年 100–300 美元。请说明 LLC 注册所在的州，以便进一步判断。
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

[The Start of Document]
"Depends on the State. In California, for example, you pay a franchise tax of $800 every year just for having LLC, and in addition to that - income tax on gross revenue. But in other States (like Wyoming, for example) there's no taxes at all, only registration fees (which may still amount to ~$100-300 a year). IRS doesn't care about LLC's at all (unless you chose to treat is as a corporation). You need to understand that in the US we have the ""Federal Government"" (IRS is part of that) and the ""State Government"" that deals with business entities, in each of the 50 States. Since you're talking about Italy, and not EU, you should similarly be talking about the relevant State, and not US."

It was not 100% clear if you have held all of these stocks for over a year.  Therefore, depending on your income tax bracket, it might make sense to hold on to the stock until you have held the individual stock for a year to only be taxed at long-term capital gains rates.  Also, you need to take into account the Net Investment Income Tax(NIIT), if your current modified adjusted income is above the current threshold.  Beyond these, I would think that you would want to apply the same methodology that caused you to buy these in the first place, as it seems to be working well for you. 2 & 3. No.  You trigger a taxable event and therefore have to pay capital gains tax on any gains.  If you have a loss in the stock and repurchase the stock within 30 days, you don't get to recognize the loss and have to add the loss to your basis in the stock (Wash Sales Rules).

You're misunderstanding the concept of retirement savings. IRA distributions are taxed, in their entirety, as ordinary income. If you withdraw before the retirement age, additional 10% penalty is added. Investment income has preferential treatment - long term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at lower rates than ordinary income. However, IRA contributions are tax deductible. I.e.: you don't pay taxes on the amounts contributed to the IRA when you earned the money, only when you withdraw. In the mean time, the money is growing, tax free, based on your investments. Anything inside the IRA is tax free, including dividends, distributions (from funds to your IRA, not from IRA to you), capital gains, etc. This is very powerful, when taking into account the compounding effect of reinvesting your dividends/sale proceeds without taking a chunk out for taxes. Consider you make an investment in a fund that appreciated 100% in half a year. You cash out to reinvest in something less
